entities.name: Boetius of Dacia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Boetius of Dacia, a prominent 13th-century Danish philosopher and Master of Arts at the University of Paris, emerged as a leading exponent of Latin Averroism, a philosophical movement that sought to interpret Aristotle through the commentaries of the Andalusian polymath Averroes. Active during the intellectual ferment of the High Middle Ages, Boetius challenged prevailing scholastic norms by rigorously asserting the autonomy of philosophical reason from theological dogma, a stance that profoundly influenced the discourse on faith and reason in Western thought.

His core contribution lay in his sophisticated commentaries on Aristotle and his development of a theory often characterized as "double truth," though Boetius himself rejected this label. He argued that philosophical inquiry, based on natural reason, could reach conclusions that, while logically sound, might contradict revealed theological truths. This intellectual position, articulated in works like his *De aeternitate mundi* (On the Eternity of the World) and *De summo bono* (On the Highest Good), directly contributed to the explosive philosophical debates at the University of Paris, particularly regarding the eternity of the world, the unity of the intellect, and the nature of human happiness.

The radical implications of Boetius's thought, alongside that of his colleague Siger of Brabant, culminated in the infamous Condemnations of 1277 by Bishop Étienne Tempier. These condemnations targeted 219 propositions deemed heretical or dangerous, many of which reflected the Latin Averroist positions on the scope and limits of reason. Although forced to leave Paris, Boetius's intellectual legacy endured, shaping later philosophical and theological debates and subtly contributing to the eventual separation of distinct spheres for science and religion.
